entry: American fantasy [[Sitcom|sitcom]] (1964–1972). It follows a witch, Samantha Stephens, who marries an ordinary mortal, Darrin, and vows to lead the life of a typical suburban housewife. Created by Sol Saks, it starred [[Elizabeth Montgomery]] as Samantha and ran for eight seasons on ABC. It was the second-highest-rated show in America during its debut season. [[Hanna-Barbera]] produced its opening and closing animation credits, and in 2002 TV Guide ranked it No. 50 among its 50 Greatest TV Shows of All Time.

American singer, songwriter, actress and businesswoman. She rose to fame as lead singer of [[Destiny's Child]] in the late 1990s. Her solo debut album, *Dangerously in Love* (2003), became one of the best-selling albums of the 21st century, and *Lemonade* (2016) was the best-selling album of 2016. She has received a record 35 [[Grammy Awards]], and she is one of the best-selling music artists of all time, with estimated sales of over 200 million records.

Indian mathematician and [[Astronomy|astronomer]], also known as Bhāskarāchārya. He is said to have headed the astronomical observatory at Ujjain, then the leading mathematical center of medieval India. His main work, *Siddhānta Śiromaṇi* ("Crown of Treatises"), was written in 1150 and is divided into four parts: *Līlāvatī* on [[Arithmetic]], *Bījagaṇita* on [[Algebra]], *Grahagaṇita* on planetary mathematics, and *Golādhyāya* on spheres. His works are noted for careful organization, clear exposition and worked examples. He has been called the greatest mathematician of medieval India, and he built on the work of [[Brahmagupta]]. His grandson Caṅgadeva founded a school in 1207 to study his works.

Hindu scripture forming part of the epic *Mahabharata*. Likely composed in the 2nd or 1st century BCE, it is regarded as a composite work by several authors, though it is traditionally attributed to the sage Veda Vyasa. It is set as a dialogue between the Pandava prince Arjuna and his charioteer [[Krishna]], an avatar of [[Vishnu]], on the battlefield at the start of the Kurukshetra War. Arjuna hesitates to fight, and Krishna urges him to perform his duty (dharma) as a warrior while attributing his actions to God. The text combines [[Yoga]] with knowledge (*jnana*) and devotion (*bhakti*), and it draws on the [[Upanishads]]. It is a central text of the [[Vedanta]] and Vaishnava traditions, and commentators including Shankara and [[Ramanuja]] have offered differing interpretations.

Classical [[India|Indian]] dance form from [[Tamil Nadu]]. It expresses South Indian religious themes, particularly of [[Shaivism]], and is performed for Nataraja, the god of dance. Its precursors are described in the *Natya Shastra*. The dance was formerly known as Sadiraattam until it was renamed Bharatanatyam in 1932. The colonial British government banned Sadiraattam in 1910, but the Indian community protested and expanded performance beyond temples in the 20th century. The style is noted for a fixed upper torso, bent knees (*aramandi*) and a gestural vocabulary of hands, eyes and face. A performance usually lasts two hours and combines *nritta* (pure dance), *nritya* (expression through gesture) and *natya* (drama). The Thanjavur Quartet formalized its modern structure.

Hindu nationalist political party in [[India]], one of the two major Indian parties alongside the [[Indian National Congress]]. It has organizational and ideological links to the [[Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh]] (RSS). Under [[Narendra Modi]], it has led the National Democratic Alliance government since 2014. It claims more than 140 million members as of 2025. Critics argue that India has experienced democratic backsliding under its rule, while supporters credit its policies with sustained economic growth and expanded welfare.

Capital city of the Indian state of [[Madhya Pradesh]]. Known as the City of Lakes for its many natural and artificial lakes, Bhopal was established by Dost Mohammad Khan, a Pashtun soldier in the Mughal army. It was the capital of the princely Bhopal State, ruled by the Nawabs of Bhopal, until India's independence in 1947, and became the capital of Madhya Pradesh in 1956. Along with [[Indore]], it is a major financial and economic center of the state. In December 1984 a pesticide plant leaked methyl isocyanate gas, causing the [[Bhopal disaster]], widely described as the worst industrial disaster in history. Bhopal was rated the cleanest state capital in India for three consecutive years, 2017 to 2019.

Gas-leak accident on December 3, 1984, at the Union Carbide India Limited pesticide plant in [[Bhopal]], India. The highly toxic gas methyl isocyanate was released, and over 500,000 people in the vicinity were exposed. The official count of immediate deaths is 2,259, while others estimate that 8,000 or more died from gas-related diseases. The plant's owner, Union Carbide Corporation, paid $470 million in 1989 to settle litigation. Civil and criminal cases were later pursued in Indian courts, and in 2010 seven former employees of the Indian subsidiary were convicted of causing death by negligence.

Capital and largest city of the Indian state of [[Odisha]], in Khordha district. Nicknamed the "Temple City", it has many temples, including Kalingan temples from the 6th to 13th centuries CE. It replaced Cuttack as capital on April 13, 1948. The modern city was designed in 1946 by German architect Otto Königsberger and, along with Jamshedpur and [[Chandigarh]], was one of India's first planned cities. Dhauli, near Bhubaneswar, was the site of the Kalinga War (c. 262–261 BCE), in which the Mauryan emperor [[Ashoka]] annexed Kalinga. The twin cities of Bhubaneswar and Cuttack had a population of 1.7 million in 2011.

King of Thailand (r. 1946–2016), titled Rama IX. Born in the United States, he spent his early life in Switzerland and succeeded his brother, King Ananda Mahidol (Rama VIII), who had died under mysterious circumstances. His reign of 70 years and 126 days was the longest of any Thai monarch. Thailand became a major US ally and regional power in Southeast Asia during his reign, and between 1985 and 1994 it was the world's fastest-growing economy according to the World Bank. The 1997 Asian financial crisis brought political instability, and periods of gradual democratization were punctuated by military coups. Activists and citizens who criticized the king or the monarchy were often forced into exile or imprisoned. He was succeeded by his son [[Vajiralongkorn]].

Landlocked kingdom in the Eastern Himalayas of [[South Asia]]. Officially the Kingdom of Bhutan, it borders China's [[Tibet Autonomous Region]] to the north and India to the south and east. Its area is 38,394 sq km and its population is over 800,000. It is a democratic constitutional monarchy, with a king as head of state and a prime minister as head of government, and [[Buddhism|Vajrayana Buddhism]] is the state religion. In the 16th century Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal unified its valleys into a single state. Bhutan was effectively a British protectorate after the Treaty of Punakha in 1910 but was never formally colonized. A 1949 treaty with India recognized each country's sovereignty, and Bhutan joined the [[United Nations]] in 1971. It has one of the world's largest water reserves for [[Hydropower|hydropower]].

Disproportionate weight in favor of or against an idea or thing, usually in a way that is inaccurate, closed-minded, prejudicial or unfair. Biases may be innate or learned, and people may hold them toward an individual, a group or a belief. In science and engineering, bias is a systematic error. [[Statistics|Statistical]] bias results from unfair [[Sampling (statistics)|sampling]] of a population or from an estimation process that does not give accurate results on average. In psychology, [[Cognition|cognitive]] biases such as confirmation bias, the tendency to favor information that fits existing beliefs, are often interpreted as [[Heuristic|heuristics]] that are adaptive for quick decisions but can systematically distort judgment. Most such studies have used Western, educated, industrialized, rich and democratic (WEIRD) populations, though cross-cultural research is emerging.

Winter sport combining cross-country skiing and [[Rifle|rifle]] shooting. It developed from military patrol exercises that began in 19th-century [[Scandinavia]] and originated in ski warfare; in the Nordic languages it is called "ski-shooting". Races cover a cross-country trail divided into shooting rounds, or bouts, which have no time limit. Missed shots add extra distance or time to a competitor's total, depending on the competition. Military patrol appeared as a demonstration event at the 1924 Chamonix Winter Olympics, and women's events were added to the Olympic program in 1992 at Albertville. The International Biathlon Union, founded in 1993, governs the sport, and [[Norway]] has won the most Olympic medals in it.

Cultural region of the [[Southern United States]], together with the Midwestern state of Missouri and the Mid-Atlantic states of Virginia and West Virginia, where evangelical [[Protestantism]] has a strong social and cultural influence. Residents show higher church attendance and greater emphasis on traditional religious values than elsewhere in the country. Arkansas has the highest proportion of evangelical Protestants, at 50%. The term was used by journalist H. L. Mencken in 1924, and in 1927 Mencken claimed it as his invention.

Family of archaic-looking [[Actinopterygii|ray-finned fishes]], the only family in the order Polypteriformes. Bichirs and the reedfish make up Polypteridae, which includes two genera, *Polypterus* and *Erpetoichthys*, with 14 species. All occur in freshwater habitats in tropical [[Africa]] and the Nile River system, mostly in swampy, shallow floodplains and estuaries. Bichirs and their fossil relatives are considered the sister group to all other living ray-finned fishes, and they likely diverged at least 330 million years ago. Their swim bladder serves as an accessory organ for air breathing. The oldest polypterids are around 100 million years old, from the early Late [[Cretaceous]] of South America and Africa. Bichirs are popular in the [[Aquarium|aquarium]] trade.

Italian neorealist drama film (1948) directed by [[Vittorio De Sica]]. Adapted by Cesare Zavattini from Luigi Bartolini's 1946 novel, it follows a poor father, Antonio Ricci, who searches postwar [[Rome]] for his stolen bicycle, which he needs for a job that is to be the salvation of his young family. His son Bruno accompanies him on the search. The film was shot on location with largely nonprofessional actors, including Lamberto Maggiorani as the father and Enzo Staiola as the son. It received an Academy Honorary Award, and in 1952 the *Sight & Sound* poll of filmmakers and critics named it the greatest film of all time. In a later poll by the same magazine, it ranked sixth.

South Korean boy band formed by YG Entertainment. Its current members are G-Dragon, Taeyang and Daesung, and it was originally a five-piece group. Dubbed the "Kings of [[K-pop]]", the group helped spread the Korean Wave internationally. Its fourth EP, *Tonight* (2011), won the inaugural Best Worldwide Act Award at the 2011 MTV Europe Music Awards. Its four Japanese studio albums were all certified gold by the Recording Industry Association of Japan.

Nickname of the Great Bell of the clock at the [[Palace of Westminster]] in London, and by extension of the clock tower housing it. The tower, originally named the Clock Tower, was renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012 for the Diamond Jubilee of Queen [[Elizabeth II]]. Designed by Augustus Pugin and Charles Barry in Perpendicular Gothic style, it was completed in 1859 and stands 316 feet (96 m) tall. The clock is known for its reliability. It is a British cultural icon and a symbol of parliamentary democracy, designated a [[World Heritage Site]] by [[UNESCO]] in 1987.

Hypothetical scenario for the ultimate fate of the universe, in which expansion reverses and the universe recollapses. The idea dates to 1922, when Russian physicist Alexander Friedmann showed in his equations that the universe could either expand or contract, depending on its density. Gravity would reverse the expansion, and the universe would end in a fireball of near-infinite temperature, possibly followed by a new [[Big Bang]]. Most available evidence, however, indicates that the hypothesis is incorrect. Observations show that the expansion of the universe is accelerating, which makes a Big Chill more likely.

Asterism of seven bright stars in the constellation Ursa Major, known as the Plough in the United Kingdom and Ireland. Four stars form a "bowl" and three form a "handle". Its two front stars, Merak and Dubhe, point to Polaris, the North Star, which makes the asterism useful in [[Celestial navigation|celestial navigation]]. In Greco-Roman tradition it is linked to the story of Callisto, transformed into a bear by [[Hera]].

Mathematical notation that describes the approximate size of a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] on a domain. The O stands for *Ordnung*, meaning order of approximation. Paul Bachmann proposed the notation in 1894, and Edmund Landau extended it in 1909; it is part of the wider Bachmann–Landau family of notations. Big O gives an upper bound on how a function grows as its variable becomes large. In [[Computer science|computer science]] it classifies algorithms by how their run time or space requirements grow with input size.

Mythical, large, hairy humanoid creature, also called Sasquatch. It is said to inhabit forests in [[North America]], particularly the [[Pacific Northwest]], and has been a cultural icon since the mid-20th century. Enthusiasts have offered sightings, photographs, recordings, hair samples and footprint casts as evidence. Scientists dismiss the creature as not a real living animal, attributing the evidence to folklore, misidentification and hoax. Similar creatures appear worldwide, such as the [[Yeti]] of Asia.

State in eastern India, bordered by Nepal to the north and Jharkhand to the south. The [[Ganges]] flows across the state from west to east, and its capital is [[Patna]]. Bihar is the 12th largest Indian state by area and the 14th largest by GDP in 2024. It played a central role in the development of [[Buddhism]]: according to tradition, the Buddha attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, and Nalanda and Vikramashila became major centers of Buddhist learning. Under the Mauryas and Guptas, Buddhism received royal patronage. Since the late 1970s, Bihar has lagged behind other Indian states in social and economic development. Economists and social scientists claim this is a direct result of central government policies, including the freight equalization policy and the Permanent Settlement of 1793 by the British [[East India Company]]. The state government credits improved governance with an economic revival.

Two-piece women's [[Swimsuit|swimsuit]], with a top that covers the breasts and a bottom that covers the pelvis and some or all of the buttocks. French designer Louis Réard introduced the modern bikini in July 1946 and named it after the [[Bikini Atoll]], where a nuclear bomb had been tested four days earlier. Once considered controversial, it was banned from beaches in several countries, including France in 1949. Film stars such as [[Brigitte Bardot]] helped gain acceptance, and by the mid-1960s the minimalist design was common in most Western countries.

Coral atoll in the [[Marshall Islands]], consisting of 23 islands around a central lagoon of 594.1 sq km. After the Second World War the United States chose it as a nuclear weapon testing site and forcibly relocated its 167 residents. The U.S. carried out 22–23 additional nuclear tests there until 1958. The islanders remain prohibited from returning because of contamination. The atoll is now a [[World Heritage Site]], remembered for its role in the Cold War.
